qrdBas-c49491-d1e101.summary: Rubric introducing the single question on distinction 23 of Book 3.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e108.summary: States the question: whether some habit, called infused faith, is necessary for the act of believing what belongs to faith.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e124.summary: First argument for the affirmative: supernatural acting presupposes supernatural being; believing the articles of faith is a supernatural act, since nature does not reach knowledge that God is triune and one; so it presupposes supernatural being in the intellect, which can only be through a habit.
claims: Supernatural action presupposes a supernatural principle.
Believing the articles is a supernatural act beyond nature's reach.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e142.summary: Second argument for the affirmative: a supernatural habit, charity, is necessarily required in the wayfarer for meritoriously loving God; infused faith in the intellect is equally necessary as charity in the will.
claims: Charity is necessary for meritorious love of God.
Infused faith stands to the intellect as charity to the will.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e156.summary: Third argument for the affirmative: neither the faith nor the sayings of the saints posit anything in vain; the saints hold infused faith necessary for believing, since without faith it is impossible to please God (Hebrews 11). The paragraph ends with the opening words of the following contrary argument, displaced in the witness.
claims: The authority of the saints posits infused faith as necessary for believing.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e169.summary: Argument to the contrary: no infused habit is needed for the act of loving God for his own sake and above all things, since the will can do this from pure naturals following the dictate of right natural reason; likewise no supernatural infused habit seems needed for believing God. The paragraph closes by introducing the plan.
claims: The will can love God above all from pure naturals.
By parity the intellect can believe God without an infused habit.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e191.summary: First point of the plan: whether an infused habit of faith must be posited in us.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e198.summary: Second point of the plan: whether, together with that infused habit, an acquired habit of faith must also be posited.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e205.summary: Third point of the plan: whether acquired and infused faith are in the intellect.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e210.summary: Final point of the plan: replies to the principal arguments.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e213.summary: Opens the first article by stating an opinion: the habit of infused faith must necessarily be posited for the act of believing what the faithful hold, just as, in their way, its holders posit that infused charity in the will is necessary for meritoriously loving God.
claims: According to this opinion, infused faith is necessary for the act of believing, as infused charity is for meritorious love.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e229.summary: Introduces the several arguments adduced for this opinion by its various proponents.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e234.summary: First argument for the opinion: firmly and immovably believing what exceeds the capacity of natural light requires a supernatural habit in the believer, since acting firmly and immovably belongs to habit (Ethics 2), and regarding the supernatural only a supernatural habit suffices; such a habit regarding things to be believed can only be faith.
claims: Firm and immovable operation is the mark of a habit.
Assent to what exceeds natural light requires a supernatural habit.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e256.summary: Second argument: as the light of glory stands to beatific vision in the homeland, so the light of faith stands to the act of believing in this life. But the light of glory is simply necessary for beatific vision, since natural light does not suffice: our intellect is to the most manifest things as the owl's eye to the sun's light (Metaphysics 2).
claims: The light of faith is to belief as the light of glory is to vision.
The light of glory is simply necessary for beatific vision.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e276.summary: Third argument: the act of believing is the most perfect act of adhesion to its object, the believer adhering more firmly than any knower, as shown by the believer's readiness to risk life and head, which a mere knower never does. Such adhesion must come from a habit, and not an acquired one, since a convert immediately adheres to the point of martyrdom without having had time to acquire a habit.
claims: Faith involves the firmest adhesion, exceeding that of science.
Willingness to die for the faith shows firmness of adhesion.
A new convert's firm adhesion cannot come from an acquired habit.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e298.summary: Fourth argument: as said in Book 1, it was necessary to reveal to man some doctrine he could not reach by natural light, since by natural powers the intellect would remain neutral, doubtful, or deny what belongs to faith; this doctrine seems to be the doctrine of faith, and especially infused faith.
claims: Supernatural revelation was necessary because natural reason cannot reach the truths of faith.
Left to nature, the intellect would be neutral, doubtful, or negative about the faith.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e315.summary: Fifth argument: what first distinguishes the believer from the unbeliever must be posited in believers; this is infused, not acquired, faith, since unbelievers and heretics can have acquired faith about many articles and credibles.
claims: Infused faith is what first distinguishes believer from unbeliever.
Unbelievers and heretics can have acquired faith about many articles.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e331.summary: Sixth argument: in a human tending to a supernatural end and object, there must be, on the side of the intellect as well as affection, some participation in that end and some supernatural directive toward it; the wayfarer must so tend to something supernatural for salvation.
claims: Ordination to a supernatural end requires a supernatural participation in the intellect.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e347.summary: Notes that many authorities of Scripture and the saints seem to support this opinion, but omits them for brevity. The paragraph ends with words introducing Bassolis's own response.
concepts: authority of Scripture and the saints

qrdBas-c49491-d1e363.summary: Bassolis's first thesis: speaking of absolute necessity, no infused habit called faith is necessary in the wayfarer even for attaining the supernatural end; absolutely, a person could attain their end without any such habit. First proof: what the wayfarer can do without in firmly assenting to known credibles is not necessary for the act of believing; but absolutely the wayfarer can firmly assent to credibles heard or narrated by someone they consider truthful, having no evidence of the thing but only testimony. Just as one firmly assents to deeds narrated by historians considered diligent and truthful, there seems no reason one could not so assent to the Gospel or the articles without any infused habit.
claims: Infused faith is not absolutely necessary for the act of believing or for attaining the supernatural end.
Firm assent can rest on testimony without evidence.
Assent to the Gospel can, absolutely, be like assent to trustworthy historians.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e415.summary: Second proof: one can believe without what contributes nothing to believing; infused faith seems to contribute nothing to the act, neither to its substance, nor to any intrinsic mode, nor to its facility, nor to its certainty. Not to its substance, since it is neither power, object, nor what presents the object, and otherwise it could act separately; not to its intrinsic degree or intensity, since any degree is of the same ratio as the whole act and could belong to the bare power; not to facility, since a newly baptized person, though having faith, finds believing as hard as an unbaptized one; not to certainty, since the principle of the act and of its certainty are the same. We do not experience what infused faith does, and one accustomed to an object believes as certainly from pure naturals as one with infused faith.
claims: Infused faith contributes nothing to the substance, degree, facility, or certainty of the act of believing.
The newly baptized find believing no easier than the unbaptized.
The principle of an act and of its certainty are the same.
We have no experience of infused faith's contribution to belief.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e472.summary: Third proof: if infused faith were absolutely necessary for the wayfarer's act of believing, then, since the intellect can know its own act of believing, its intensity, and every mode (nothing being more certain to a person than their own faith, at least as an act), the wayfarer could know that they have the habit, as they know they have an intellectual power; but this is false and not experienced. Bassolis concedes the argument may face an objection but does not care.
claims: We know our own act of believing with certainty.
We do not know by experience that we have infused faith.
So infused faith is not a necessary principle of the act.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e495.summary: Fourth proof: the habit of infused faith is no more absolutely necessary for believing in this life than the habit of glory in the homeland; but the latter is in no way absolutely necessary, as proven in an earlier question. The paragraph ends with words introducing the summary conclusion.
claims: The habit of glory is not absolutely necessary for beatific vision.
Infused faith is no more necessary than the light of glory.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e508.summary: Summarizes the first conclusion: infused faith is not absolutely necessary for the wayfarer's act of believing; absolutely, the wayfarer can have as perfect and firm an act of believing all credibles without it as with it, just as, according to Book 1, one can love God as perfectly without infused charity as with it. A heretic adheres to their heresy, even to death, as firmly as one with infused faith adheres to truth, plainly from some purely natural cause. Faith does not supply a different knowledge of terms: believer and unbeliever have the same concepts, differing only in assent or dissent to their combination, and it is unnecessary to attribute that difference to the infused habit. This fits what was said in the second question of the prologue to Book 1 on the necessity of revelation: since even one with infused faith assents only by willing, and faith contributes nothing to the act, there is no reason why someone could not firmly assent to credibles from mere naturals by the will's command.
claims: Absolutely, belief without infused faith can be as perfect and firm as belief with it.
One can likewise love God as perfectly without infused charity.
Heretics' firm adhesion to error shows that firmness has natural causes.
Believer and unbeliever share the same concepts of terms and differ only in assent.
Assent of faith is commanded by the will and possible from pure naturals.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e584.summary: Second thesis: infused faith must in fact be posited in every wayfarer who is to be saved and in every truly baptized person at that time, so that no one is saved without faith at the end; this rests on divine ordination known from the saints and the Church's tradition. It is posited for a certain adornment, perfection, and health of the mind preceding charity in the will, but Bassolis does not see that it contributes anything to the act. To the reply that it disposes, inclines, facilitates, and firms the act, even if unperceived, he answers that he does not understand that disposition, since the intellect is sufficiently disposed as receptive by itself. He sees no ground for such claims and cannot effectively refute them, but by parsimony, posits fewer things without experience, compelling reason, or authority, and so does not attribute these conditions to faith, though he does posit faith itself on authority. The paragraph ends with words introducing the replies.
claims: By divine ordination, infused faith is in fact given to all the saved and the baptized.
Infused faith is posited for the adornment and perfection of the mind, preceding charity.
There is no evidence that infused faith disposes, facilitates, or firms the act of belief.
By parsimony, nothing should be posited without experience, compelling reason, or authority.
Infused faith itself is posited on the authority of the saints and the Church.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e641.summary: Reply to the first argument for the opinion: its major premise is denied, since one can firmly and immovably believe something about the supreme object without a supernatural habit, from a natural habit or from the will commanding the intellect to assent firmly to what is heard or narrated, which is within the will's power. The disciples' request 'Lord, increase our faith' means they knew they could do nothing without Christ and asked him to cooperate in a perfect act of faith, not that an infused habit must cooperate. That the object is supernatural does not require a supernatural habit, as the object of natural science of God is supernatural and natural friendship can have God as object.
claims: Firm belief about the supreme object is possible from a natural habit or the will's command.
Firm assent is in the power of the will.
'Increase our faith' asks for Christ's concurrence, not an infused habit.
A supernatural object does not require a supernatural habit.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e691.summary: Reply to the second argument: as said, the light of glory is not absolutely necessary for seeing God in the homeland. Our intellect is like the owl's eye to divine vision only in that by pure naturals, without God's special influence, it cannot see God clearly as it understands material things, or because of the imperfect conjunction of the present state, not because it lacks a habit.
claims: The light of glory is not absolutely necessary for the vision of God.
The intellect's incapacity for clear vision of God stems from lack of special divine influence or present conditions, not lack of a habit.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e713.summary: Reply to the third argument: so far as experience shows, the act of believing has no greater firmness of adhesion than other acts, such as adhesion to first principles, to known conclusions, to heresy or falsehood, or to a false conclusion (Ethics 7), none of which requires more than mere naturals; the same holds for faith, especially since, according to many including the opponents, natural reason can establish that God revealing cannot deceive or be deceived and should be firmly adhered to. The believer or heretic risks their life not from greater certainty than science but because they hope for a reward, which the knower does not. Faith has certainty of adhesion, but not certainty of evidence, which belongs to science.
claims: Faith's firmness of adhesion is not experienced as greater than that of other assents.
Natural reason can know that God revealing cannot deceive or be deceived.
Martyrdom reflects hope of reward, not greater certainty.
Faith has certainty of adhesion but not of evidence.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e771.summary: Reply to the fourth argument, in two ways. First: even if supernatural revelation of a doctrine was necessary at some time, what follows is not a necessary habit of faith but a necessary revelation in an act of believing or understanding, such as an actual abstractive cognition; once revealed and passed on under testimony, it can be believed from mere naturals, as faith comes by hearing (Romans 10), just as one who could not discover geometry can believe and learn it from a teacher. The credibles exceed natural light as to being seen clearly, not as to being believed on another's word. Second, since this may not fit earlier remarks: revelation of the doctrine of faith was necessary not because belief without an infused habit is impossible but because it is difficult; absolutely, having the concepts of the terms, one could firmly assent from pure naturals. Revelation was needed because God certified in an act that this is so to the one receiving revelation, and the hearer can more easily believe from pure naturals that it was revealed to that person.
claims: Necessary revelation implies a revealed cognition, not a necessary infused habit.
Revealed doctrine, once transmitted by testimony, can be believed from pure naturals.
Faith comes by hearing.
Credibles exceed natural light as to clear vision, not as to belief on testimony.
Revelation was necessary because of difficulty, not impossibility, of believing without it.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e856.summary: Reply to the fifth argument: although in fact the believer is first distinguished from the unbeliever by infused faith, at least in baptized children (adults are perhaps another matter), this is not absolutely necessary; the believer could be distinguished by the act of believing without any such habit, or by acquired faith, in which case a child lacking both would not be called a believer.
claims: De facto, baptized children are distinguished as believers by infused faith.
Absolutely, the act of belief or acquired faith could distinguish believer from unbeliever.
Without infused faith a child lacking act and acquired habit would not be a believer.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e878.summary: Reply to the sixth argument: the act of believing or a habit acquired from pure naturals is a sufficient participation on the intellect's side regarding the supernatural object or end; no infused habit is necessarily required for believing, as no infused charity is necessarily required in the will, though by the divine ordination we hold, both infused charity and infused faith are to be posited. Ends the first article.
claims: Natural acts and acquired habits of belief suffice as intellectual participation in the supernatural end.
By divine ordination both infused faith and infused charity are nonetheless posited.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e902.summary: Opens the second article with the view that, given the infused habit of faith in the intellect, acquired faith should not be posited in us.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e913.summary: First argument: if acquired faith were posited with infused faith about the same object, two accidents of the same kind would coexist in the same subject, since habits with the same object and subject are of the same kind; but this is impossible (Metaphysics 5), especially for absolute accidents.
claims: Habits with the same object and subject are of the same kind.
Two accidents of the same kind cannot coexist in the same subject.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e929.summary: Second argument: when a more perfect habit of the same kind arrives or remains, the less perfect does not remain but either yields or combines into one habit with the more perfect; infused faith is more perfect and of the same kind.
claims: A less perfect habit of the same kind yields to or merges with a more perfect one.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e943.summary: Third argument: if both habits coexist, how do they relate to the act of believing? Not equally, since the infused is nobler; not with the infused as more principal, since it contributes nothing to the act (as Bassolis himself held); hence neither can the acquired be said to be more or less principal. Since they cannot relate to the act together in any way, they should not be posited together.
claims: There is no coherent account of how infused and acquired faith would jointly cause the act of belief.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e965.summary: Fourth argument: if someone had perfectly acquired geometry, infusing geometry in them would be pointless; conversely, if perfect faith is infused, acquiring faith is pointless. The same argument would exclude acquired charity in one with infused charity. The paragraph ends with words introducing the reply.
claims: A perfect infused habit makes a corresponding acquired habit superfluous.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e991.summary: Bassolis's thesis: notwithstanding these arguments, acquired faith must be posited in adults, a habit generated by frequent acts of believing, just as natural friendship is acquired by frequent acts of loving, despite infused faith or charity.
claims: Adults have acquired faith generated by repeated acts of believing.
Acquired faith coexists with infused faith as natural friendship with infused charity.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1004.summary: First proof: facility in or toward the act of believing is the sign of a generated habit (Ethics 2); we experience that some are prone and believe what belongs to faith easily, and this is not through the infused habit, as shown.
claims: Facility is the sign of a generated habit.
Experienced facility in believing comes from acquired, not infused, faith.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1017.summary: Second proof from Augustine, Against the Letter of the Foundation (against Mani): 'I would not believe the Gospel unless I believed the Church', and he rejects the Nazarenes' gospel because the Church does not receive it. This would mean nothing unless acquired faith could be had from the Church's testimony.
claims: Augustine's dictum presupposes acquired faith grounded on the Church's testimony.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1033.summary: Third proof: a Jewish or Saracen child raised among Christians from infancy could believe the articles as a Christian child does, not through infused faith, which they would not have; so acquired faith should also be posited in the Christian adult, even granting they have infused faith.
claims: An unbaptized child raised among Christians could believe the articles as well as a Christian child.
Such belief comes from acquired faith, which must also be posited in Christian adults.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1050.summary: Fourth proof: Paul argues, 'How shall they believe him of whom they have not heard?' and concludes 'faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ' (Romans 10). One with infused faith can hear and believe God's word no less than one without, and so can acquire faith equally; Paul speaks of acquired faith, since charity, and therefore faith, is not necessarily infused upon hearing God's word, for God never first infuses faith without charity, though he may preserve it unformed without charity.
claims: Romans 10 speaks of acquired faith from hearing.
One with infused faith can acquire faith by hearing as well as one without.
God never first infuses faith without charity, though unformed faith may remain.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1079.summary: Fifth proof: someone with infused faith about everything may become a heretic about one article yet firmly and habitually adhere to the others, but not by the infused habit, which though compatible with all other sins, even hatred of God, the greatest, is commonly held incompatible with heresy and the sin of unbelief. So before, alongside infused faith, they had acquired faith about those articles. The paragraph ends with words introducing the conclusion.
claims: Infused faith is compatible with every sin except heresy and unbelief.
A heretic's habitual adherence to the other articles comes from acquired faith.
Hatred of God is the greatest sin.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1101.summary: Concludes the first thesis: in adults, a habit of acquired faith is generated by acts of believing notwithstanding infused faith.
claims: Acquired faith is generated in adults by acts of believing despite the presence of infused faith.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1108.summary: Second thesis: infused and acquired faith are not of the same kind, just as infused and acquired charity are not. First proof: habits are not of the same kind if nature cannot attain one, which is simply supernatural and caused immediately by God alone, while nature can attain and cause the other.
claims: Infused and acquired faith differ in kind, as do infused and acquired charity.
A habit caused immediately by God alone differs in kind from one nature can cause.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1128.summary: Second proof: habits are not of the same kind if one facilitates an act and the other does not; acquired faith, as experienced, facilitates believing, while infused faith does not.
claims: Acquired faith facilitates belief; infused faith does not; so they differ in kind.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1139.summary: Third proof: infused faith is had before any repetition of acts, whereas acquired faith presupposes and is generated by repeated acts, by which infused faith cannot be generated, as neither can charity.
claims: Infused faith precedes acts; acquired faith is generated by them.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1151.summary: Note: God could infuse a faith numerically or specifically the same as that which is acquired; but it would not be of the same kind as the faith now infused, but simply of another kind, as acquired faith is from infused. The paragraph ends with words introducing the replies.
claims: God could infuse a habit identical in kind to acquired faith.
Such a habit would differ in kind from the faith actually infused.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1171.summary: Reply to the first argument: positing acquired with infused faith does not place two accidents of the same kind in one subject, since they differ in kind. Granting they share subject and object, they are not therefore the same kind, since, as said in Book 1, the same subject can have habits and cognitions of different kinds regarding the same object, as abstractive and intuitive cognition of the same object. Even if they were of the same kind, it does not follow that they could not coexist in the same subject.
claims: Sameness of subject and object does not entail sameness of kind.
Abstractive and intuitive cognitions of the same object differ in kind.
Even habits of the same kind can coexist in one subject.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1206.summary: Reply to the second argument: the two habits are not of the same kind and cannot constitute or merge into one habit. Even if they were, one need not yield or merge with the other, just as two lights in the medium do not become one light but remain distinct in the same part of the medium, and two species of two individuals of the same kind coexist in the imagination or in an angelic intellect, as said in Book 2.
claims: Infused and acquired faith cannot merge into one habit.
Even same-kind forms can coexist distinctly in one subject, as two lights in a medium or two species in an intellect.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1228.summary: Reply to the third argument begins: infused faith does nothing toward the act, but acquired faith does facilitate it; the paragraph turns to the objection that infused faith is nobler and more perfect.
claims: Only acquired faith contributes to the act of believing, by facilitating it.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1237.summary: Continues the reply: infused faith is nobler in itself but not in relation to this act. To the objection that a habit that is not a principle of action is posited in vain, Bassolis denies this of every habit, such as the infused habit, which is posited for the adornment and perfection of the creature to which it is infused, and so not in vain.
claims: Infused faith is nobler in itself but not as related to the act.
A habit need not be a principle of action to be posited not in vain.
Infused habits exist for the adornment and perfection of the creature.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1250.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: the infused faith we posit is not of the same kind as acquired faith, so neither is superfluous; and even if they were the same kind, neither would be superfluous, since a person is perfected in more ways by several habits than by one. Ends the second article.
claims: Since they differ in kind, neither infused nor acquired faith is superfluous.
Even same-kind habits perfect a person more fully together.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1267.summary: States the third article: whether acquired and infused faith are both in the intellect as their subject.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1276.summary: Arguments that faith is not in the intellect as subject: unbelief, being a sin, is in the will, not the intellect; Augustine says one can do other things unwillingly but cannot believe except willingly, so faith is in the will; and the act of believing is meritorious, while merit belongs principally to the will.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1294.summary: Bassolis's thesis: all faith, infused or acquired, is in the intellect as its subject, because faith is an intellectual cognitive habit; because it is not a habit of the will, which would be one of loving or hating; and because believing is an elicited act of the intellect, not the will, as is believing principles and demonstrated conclusions.
claims: Both infused and acquired faith are in the intellect as subject.
Faith is a cognitive, not appetitive, habit.
Believing is an act elicited by the intellect.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1314.summary: Confirms from Augustine that believing is an act of the intellect: to believe is nothing but to think with assent, and thinking belongs to the intellect. Whether to the speculative or practical intellect is referred to the last question of the prologue to Book 1 (whether theology is practical or speculative), where some things said about infused faith are modified by the present question, as are some in the first question of that prologue. The paragraph then replies to the first objection: unbelief involves two things, error about a credible, which is in the intellect like faith, and willing to err, defend error, or neglect to abandon it, which is formally the sin and is in the will but is not formally opposed to faith.
claims: To believe is to think with assent, an act of the intellect.
The present question modifies earlier statements on infused faith in the Book 1 prologue.
Unbelief as error is in the intellect; unbelief as sin is in the will.
The sinful component of unbelief is not formally opposed to faith.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1360.summary: Reply to the second objection (the argument from merit): merit does not consist formally in the act of believing in itself, but in so far as it is an act commanded by the will.
claims: The act of believing is meritorious only as commanded by the will.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1369.summary: Reply to Augustine's dictum that no one believes unwillingly (noted as properly the second objection): believing still belongs to the intellect, as does faith as a habit, though the act of believing depends on the will's command, at least for what is not evident from the terms, such as the credibles of Christian faith. This distinguishes faith from 'belief' in first principles or in conclusions deduced from evident principles, if those may be called belief by extension.
claims: Belief and faith belong to the intellect even though belief depends on the will's command.
Dependence on the will holds for what is not evident from the terms.
Assent to first principles and demonstrated conclusions is belief only by extension.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1396.summary: Reply to the first principal argument: believing what belongs to faith is not a supernatural action; the intellect is capable of it by natural light, as explained and proven above.
claims: Believing the articles is not a supernatural action but within natural capacity.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1409.summary: Reply to the second principal argument on meritorious love: as said in Book 1, absolutely speaking, no infused habit of charity is required for it.
claims: Absolutely, meritorious love does not require infused charity.

qrdBas-c49491-d1e1418.summary: Reply to the third principal argument: infused faith is not in vain, being for the soul's adornment and perfection and a noble sign, though not necessary for the act of believing; how it is necessary in those to be saved was said above.
claims: Infused faith is not in vain: it adorns and perfects the soul and is a noble sign.
It is not necessary for the act of believing.

qrdBas-c49491-Dd1e218.summary: Article 1 asks whether an infused habit of faith must be posited. Against an opinion supported by six arguments (firm assent to the supernatural requires a supernatural habit; the analogy with the light of glory; faith's supreme firmness shown in the convert's martyrdom; the necessity of revelation; infused faith as what distinguishes believer from unbeliever; the need for supernatural participation in the intellect), Bassolis argues that infused faith is not absolutely necessary. Firm assent can rest on testimony, as with historians; infused faith contributes nothing experienceable to the act's substance, degree, facility, or certainty; we would otherwise know we have it; and it is no more necessary than the light of glory. Heretics adhere as firmly from natural causes, and the will can command firm assent from pure naturals. Yet by divine ordination, known from the saints and tradition, infused faith is in fact given to all the saved and baptized, for the mind's adornment and perfection; by parsimony he declines to attribute to it any disposing or facilitating role. The replies hold that faith's firmness is not greater than other assents and martyrdom reflects hope of reward; that revelation was necessary because of difficulty, not impossibility, with revealed doctrine believable from hearing; and that acts or acquired habits suffice as intellectual participation.
claims: Infused faith is not absolutely necessary for believing or for salvation.
Firm assent to the articles is possible from pure naturals, on testimony and by the will's command.
Infused faith contributes nothing experienceable to the act of believing.
By divine ordination infused faith is in fact given to all the saved and baptized, for the soul's adornment.
By parsimony, nothing beyond what experience, reason, or authority requires should be attributed to infused faith.
Faith has certainty of adhesion, not of evidence; martyrdom reflects hope of reward.
Revelation was necessary because of difficulty, not impossibility, of natural belief.

qrdBas-c49491-Dd1e915.summary: Article 2 asks whether acquired faith must be posited alongside infused faith. Against arguments that two same-kind accidents cannot coexist, that the less perfect habit yields to the more perfect, that no account of their joint causality is possible, and that an acquired habit would be superfluous, Bassolis holds that adults have acquired faith generated by repeated acts, as natural friendship coexists with charity. He proves this from experienced facility in believing, Augustine's 'I would not believe the Gospel unless I believed the Church', the Jewish or Saracen child raised among Christians, 'faith comes by hearing', and the heretic who retains the other articles after losing infused faith through heresy. Infused and acquired faith differ in kind: one is caused by God alone, does not facilitate, and precedes acts; the other is natural, facilitating, and generated by acts; God could infuse a habit like the acquired one, but it would differ from the faith now infused. The replies deny that shared subject and object entail sameness of kind, show that even same-kind forms can coexist, and hold that infused faith, though contributing nothing to the act, is not in vain, existing for the creature's adornment.
claims: Adults have acquired faith generated by repeated acts, coexisting with infused faith.
Acquired faith explains facility in believing and the heretic's retained beliefs.
Infused and acquired faith differ in kind.

Same subject and object do not entail same kind of habit.
Infused habits exist for the creature's adornment, not as principles of action.

qrdBas-c49491-Dd1e1290.summary: Article 3 asks whether infused and acquired faith are in the intellect. Against arguments that unbelief is a sin in the will, that one believes only willingly (Augustine), and that merit belongs to the will, Bassolis holds that all faith is in the intellect, since faith is a cognitive habit and believing, 'thinking with assent' (Augustine), is an elicited act of the intellect. He notes that this question modifies some claims about infused faith in the Book 1 prologue. Unbelief as error is in the intellect, and as willed error it is a sin in the will not formally opposed to faith; the act of belief is meritorious and voluntary only as commanded by the will, a dependence that holds for what is not evident from the terms, unlike assent to first principles or demonstrated conclusions.
claims: Both infused and acquired faith are in the intellect as subject.
Believing is an act elicited by the intellect and commanded by the will.
The sin of unbelief is in the will, its error in the intellect.
Merit and voluntariness attach to belief as commanded by the will.
This question corrects earlier claims about infused faith in the Book 1 prologue.

qrdBas-c49491-Dd1e1427.summary: Replies to the principal arguments: believing the articles is not a supernatural action but within the intellect's natural light; meritorious love absolutely requires no infused charity (as in Book 1); and infused faith is not posited in vain, since it adorns and perfects the soul as a noble sign, though it is not necessary for the act of believing.
claims: Believing the articles is within natural capacity.
Meritorious love absolutely does not require infused charity.
Infused faith exists for the soul's adornment, not the act of belief.

qrdBas-c49491.summary: The single question on Book 3, distinction 23 asks whether a habit called infused faith is necessary for the act of believing. Bassolis gives a strikingly minimalist account of infused faith. In Article 1 he argues that, absolutely, it is not necessary: firm assent to the articles can rest on testimony and the will's command from pure naturals, as with trusted historians; infused faith contributes nothing experienceable to the act's substance, intensity, facility, or certainty; heretics adhere as firmly from natural causes; and faith's certainty is one of adhesion, not evidence. Revelation was needed because natural belief was difficult, not impossible. Yet by divine ordination, known from the saints and tradition, infused faith is in fact given to all the saved and baptized, for the soul's adornment and perfection; by parsimony he attributes no further causal role to it. In Article 2 he holds that adults also have acquired faith generated by repeated acts, shown by facility, by the Church's testimony (Augustine), by faith from hearing, and by the heretic who retains other articles, and that infused and acquired faith differ in kind. In Article 3 he places both in the intellect, believing being an act elicited by the intellect but commanded by the will, which accounts for its merit and for the sin of unbelief. He notes that this question corrects earlier claims about infused faith in the Book 1 prologue.
claims: Infused faith is not absolutely necessary for the act of believing.
Firm belief in the articles is possible from pure naturals on testimony and by the will's command.
Infused faith contributes nothing experienceable to the act of believing.
By divine ordination infused faith is in fact given to all the saved and baptized, for the soul's adornment.
Adults have acquired faith, generated by acts, which differs in kind from infused faith.
Both infused and acquired faith are in the intellect; belief is elicited by the intellect and commanded by the will.
Revelation was necessary because natural belief was difficult, not impossible.
